content: 1. Identify and prioritize individuals at higher risk of pretreatment HIV drug resistance (HIVDR) to non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs). This includes people initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART) who have had prior exposure to NNRTIs or other groups identified as high-risk. These individuals should start a first-line ART regimen that does not include NNRTIs, without requiring pretreatment HIVDR testing. 2. Use fixed-dose combinations and age-appropriate optimal antiretroviral (ARV) formulations whenever possible. This approach enhances adherence to treatment and reduces the likelihood of selecting for HIV drug resistance. 3. Expand viral load monitoring capacity to ensure that all individuals living with HIV undergo testing. Promptly switch individuals to second-line ART when virological failure is confirmed (defined as a viral load greater than 1,000 copies/mL). 4. Strengthen interventions that promote treatment literacy and adherence support. Maximize retention in care, minimize loss to follow-up, and ensure the regular use of programmatic data to improve outcomes. 5. If other subpopulations at high risk of pretreatment HIVDR are identified, they should also be prioritized for appropriate public health interventions. Efforts must be made to minimize stigma and discrimination associated with these interventions. 6. If nationally representative pretreatment HIVDR data are available, prioritize the use of non-EFV/NVP-containing first-line ART regimens for individuals reporting prior ARV drug exposure. Consider urgently transitioning all ART starters to non-EFV/NVP regimens. 7. Introduce pretreatment HIVDR testing to guide the selection of first-line ART regimens where feasible. 8. Monitor factors associated with the emergence of HIVDR at treatment sites using quality-of-care indicators predictive of HIVDR, such as early-warning indicators. 9. Countries should strive to use nationally representative pretreatment HIVDR data as the gold standard when making changes to public health and ART program policies. These data should inform national policy changes. 10. Transitioning to non-NNRTI-based first-line ART regimens requires careful implementation considerations, as outlined in the WHO technical update on transitioning to new antiretroviral drugs in HIV programs. 11. The 2016 WHO consolidated guidelines on antiretroviral drug use recommend testing and treating all individuals diagnosed with HIV, regardless of CD4 count. The preferred first-line ART regimen for adults, adolescents, pregnant and breastfeeding women, and children aged 3–10 years is based on NNRTIs. 12. Recent studies have documented an increased prevalence of NNRTI pretreatment HIVDR exceeding 10% among individuals starting first-line ART in several lowand middle-income countries. This warrants a public health response. 13. Modeling predicts that if NNRTI pretreatment HIVDR prevalence exceeds 10% and first-line ART remains NNRTI-based, this could result in significant mortality, new HIV infections, and increased treatment costs over the next five years. 14. The guidelines recommend using alternative first-line non-NNRTI-based regimens for individuals starting ART in settings with high NNRTI pretreatment HIVDR prevalence. Pretreatment HIVDR testing should also be introduced to guide regimen selection. 15. The guidelines emphasize the importance of protecting the human rights of individuals needing HIV services, including informed consent, prevention of stigma and discrimination, and promotion of gender equity. 16. The guidelines are intended for national HIV program managers and other stakeholders, including clinicians, laboratory managers, policymakers, and community-based organizations, to support the public health response to pretreatment HIVDR.
